cards.front: In acute ICH, target SBP is < [___] mmHg (INTERACT-2), while ischaemic stroke uses permissive hypertension.
cards.context:
ICH treatment is HEAD-CONTAINMENT: lower SBP rapidly to <140 to limit haematoma expansion (INTERACT-2 NEJM 2013). Higher pressures continue to drive bleeding through fragile vessel walls.

Ischaemic stroke is the OPPOSITE: permissive hypertension to maintain perfusion of penumbra (the rescuable tissue around the infarct core). Only intervene if BP exceeds 220/120 or 185/110 if planning thrombolysis.

cards.front: VBG-to-ABG conversion offsets? pH: VBG 0.02–0.04 lower. pCO₂: VBG [___] higher. HCO₃⁻: Essentially same. Lactate: Same. PaO₂: Cannot assess from VBG.
cards.context:
VBG correlates well for pH, pCO₂, lactate, electrolytes. Main limitation: cannot assess PaO₂.

Use SpO₂ for oxygenation screening; ABG only when precise PaO₂/P:F ratio needed.

cards.front: Tramadol's two unique risks: serotonin syndrome and lowered [___] threshold.
cards.context: Tramadol's serotonergic activity can precipitate serotonin syndrome with SSRIs/SNRIs. It also lowers seizure threshold independently — avoid in epilepsy or with other pro-convulsant drugs.

cards.front: The minimum possible GCS score is 3 and maximum is [___].
cards.context: GCS 3 is the minimum (E1V1M1). GCS 15 is the maximum (E4V5M6).

cards.front: Metformin is withheld on the day of surgery due to risk of lactic [___].
cards.context: Managing medications perioperatively is a key preoperative assessment skill. Some drugs must continue, others must be withheld.

cards.front: Normal ionised calcium range is [___] mmol/L.
cards.context:
Ionised calcium is the physiologically active fraction (~50% of total Ca²⁺); the rest is bound to albumin.

Low iCa (<1.12) causes paraesthesia, tetany, and prolonged QT; massive transfusion (citrate chelation), pancreatitis, and renal failure are common ICU triggers.

cards.front: In acute pancreatitis, [___] >150 mg/L at 48 hours predicts severe disease and necrosis.
cards.context:
CRP rises in pancreatitis as the inflammatory response peaks at 48-72 h.

Persistent elevation or rising trend prompts CT for necrosis assessment and HDU/ICU referral. Day 1 CRP is *not* useful — wait for the 48-h value.

cards.front: After a significant overdose of an analgesic that targets COX but has a narrow hepatic-safety margin, management includes: check paracetamol levels at 4 hours, start [___] if indicated by the nomogram, and arrange psychiatric review before discharge.
cards.context:
Paracetamol overdose looks deceptively boring in the first 24 h — nausea, vague abdominal discomfort, normal observations and LFTs. Hepatic injury declares itself at 24-72 h, often after the patient has been discharged.

Protocol: plot serum paracetamol drawn at 4+ h post-ingestion (earlier values can't be interpreted) on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram; above the line.

cards.front: First-line vasodilator in acute pulmonary oedema is GTN, started [___] then titrated as an IV infusion.
cards.context:
GTN works on both sides of the cardiac equation in APO: low doses venodilate (drops preload), higher doses arteriodilate (drops afterload).

Sequence: SL GTN 400-800 µg q5min while gaining IV access, then IV GTN 10-20 µg/min titrated up to 200 µg/min.

cards.front: Massive PE with persistent hypotension: systemic [___] mg alteplase IV over 2 hours.
cards.context:
Massive PE = obstruction killing the patient haemodynamically (sustained hypotension or vasopressor need despite fluid).

Alteplase 100 mg over 2 h is standard; in cardiac arrest from suspected PE, 50 mg bolus + continue CPR 60-90 min.

cards.front: Parkland timing is calculated from time of injury (not presentation). The first half is given over [___] hours, the second half over 16 hours.
cards.context: Capillary leak is maximal in the first 8 hours post-burn, so fluid requirements are frontloaded. Timing from injury (not presentation) matters — delayed patients need catch-up fluids to compensate for initial deficit.

cards.front: Severe exercise-associated hyponatraemia (EAH) with seizures: give [___] mL of 3% hypertonic saline IV over 10 min.
cards.context: Severe EAH with encephalopathy is a medical emergency. The 100 mL bolus of 3% saline raises sodium by approximately 2-3 mmol/L — enough to reduce cerebral oedema without overcorrecting.

cards.front: Each digoxin Fab vial binds approximately [___] mg of digoxin; empiric dosing if amount unknown is 10 vials.
cards.context:
Digoxin Fab fragments (Digibind/DigiFab) bind digoxin and are renally excreted as inert complexes. Each vial neutralises ~0.5 mg.

When the ingested amount is unknown and the patient is unstable, give 10 vials empirically — this covers the LD50 and is cheaper than missing the antidote.

Indications: K⁺ >5.0, ventricular arrhythmias, bradyarrhythmias unresponsive to atropine, or ingestion >10 mg (adult) / >4 mg (child).

cards.front: A fentanyl patch at 25 mcg/hour is equivalent to approximately [___] mg oral morphine per day.
cards.context:
The 25-mcg/h patch ≈ 60 mg/day oral morphine equivalent. Useful conversions: 12 mcg/h ≈ 30 mg/day, 50 mcg/h ≈ 120 mg/day.

Fentanyl is preferred over morphine in renal impairment (no active metabolites) and over patches over oral when swallowing is impaired or compliance is unreliable.

cards.front: Tramadol's two unique risks: [___] syndrome and lowered seizure threshold.
cards.context: Tramadol's serotonergic activity can precipitate serotonin syndrome with SSRIs/SNRIs. It also lowers seizure threshold independently — avoid in epilepsy or with other pro-convulsant drugs.

cards.front: A non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min delivers approximately 85% FiO₂; only a [___] with reservoir can approach 100%.
cards.context: Despite having one-way valves and a reservoir bag, the non-rebreather mask cannot achieve 100% FiO2 because air leaks in around the mask edges (imperfect seal).

cards.front: Echo signs of massive PE: dilated RV compressing LV with septal bowing (the D-sign). Specific but insensitive: McConnell's sign (akinetic RV free wall with preserved apex). Normal RV : LV ratio is [___].
cards.context:
In massive PE, the RV dilates and compresses the LV. Normally the RV is 2/3 the size of the LV — in massive PE the RV is bigger.

The interventricular septum bows toward the LV (D-sign). McConnell's sign (akinetic RV free wall with preserved apex) is specific but insensitive.

cards.front: Anion gap formula: AG = Na − ([___] + HCO₃). Normal range is 8–12 mmol/L.
cards.context:
The anion gap captures unmeasured anions — primarily albumin (~2.4 mmol/L per 10 g/L), with phosphate, lactate, ketones, and toxin metabolites filling the rest in disease.

Without the correction, a sepsis patient with albumin of 20 looks like 'normal AG' when they actually have a meaningful HAGMA.

cards.front: Gallstone pancreatitis complicated by cholangitis (Charcot's triad) requires urgent [___] within 24 hours.
cards.context:
The combination of biliary obstruction + ascending infection is what kills in cholangitis — bile stasis allows enteric bacteria to translocate into the bloodstream.

ERCP within 24 hours decompresses the obstructed duct, drains the infected bile, and removes the offending stone in a single intervention; surgery alone without source control has unacceptable mortality.

cards.front: The defining spirometry feature of obstructive lung disease is an FEV₁/FVC ratio below [___].
cards.context:
Obstructive lung disease: FEV1/FVC ratio under 0.7 with a scooped (concave) expiratory flow-volume loop. FEV1 falls more than FVC.

Bronchodilator reversibility (≥12% + 200 mL improvement) supports asthma; absence indicates fixed COPD.

cards.front: In young trauma patients, BP may remain normal until ~[___]% blood volume loss.
cards.context: Young patients have excellent compensatory mechanisms (vasoconstriction, tachycardia) that maintain BP despite significant blood loss — but once they decompensate, it happens suddenly and dramatically.

cards.front: CRASH-2 showed TXA benefit only within [___] hours of injury; after this window there is possible harm.
cards.context:
CRASH-2 (2010, 20,000 trauma patients) found tranexamic acid (1 g over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 hours) reduces all-cause mortality and bleeding deaths if given within 3 hours of injury.

After 3 hours, TXA may HARM — possibly through paradoxical bleeding from secondary fibrinolysis activation. Document time of injury, not time of presentation. Don't give TXA late.

cards.front: Normal arterial lactate is < [___] mmol/L.
cards.context:
VBG values are offset from ABG: pH ~0.03 lower, pCO₂ ~6 higher. HCO₃ and lactate are the same.

PaO₂ cannot be assessed on VBG.
